Breaking Barriers in Law School and Family Life.
Law school in the 1950s wasn’t exactly a place that rolled out the welcome mat for women. When Ruth showed up at Harvard, she was one of only a few women in a sea of hundreds of men. The message was loud and clear—she didn’t really belong.
Imagine this: the dean invites the women to dinner, and instead of a warm welcome, he asks why they think they deserve to take a man’s place. That’s the kind of moment that could make anyone want to disappear. But not Ruth. She just sat up, a little taller, determined to prove she absolutely belonged there.
The obstacles kept coming. Study groups often left her out, and sometimes professors dismissed her questions without a second thought. But Ruth? She had her own way of doing things. She pored over every single case, prepared down to the smallest detail, and let her work speak for itself.
Home wasn’t any less challenging. Marty, her husband, was also in law school, and when he got seriously ill, Ruth’s world became a delicate balancing act. She cared for their young daughter, managed the house, and kept up with coursework for both herself and Marty. Nights blurred into mornings as she typed up Marty’s papers after finishing her own—running on coffee, determination, and love for her family.
Most people would’ve cracked under all that pressure, but Ruth found her rhythm. She learned how to focus on one thing at a time, to lean on the rare people who truly supported her, and to keep moving forward. When Marty recovered, it was a huge relief—but it also deepened their sense of partnership. He was her biggest cheerleader, never threatened by her ambition, always ready with a joke to lighten the mood. Their marriage was a real partnership—something you didn’t see much back then—and it gave Ruth the confidence to keep reaching higher.
When Marty’s job took them to New York, Ruth transferred to Columbia and graduated at the very top of her class. But even with all those credentials, doors stayed shut. Law firms wouldn’t hire her, judges turned down her clerkship applications—all because she was a woman and a mother. That’s when Ruth realized: talent alone wasn’t going to be enough. The system itself was set up to keep women out.
Instead of letting bitterness take over, she turned to a new path. Ruth found work as a researcher and teacher, diving deep into the ways law treated men and women differently. Every setback became fuel for her growing sense of purpose.
During these years, Ruth’s understanding of justice really took root. She saw how the law could be both a shield and a weapon, and she started to imagine how it could open doors for people who’d always found them closed.
The lessons of persistence, true partnership, and quiet determination? They became her trademarks—guiding the way she’d go on to fight for change, not just for herself, but for everyone after her.
